name: Gārgī Vāchaknavī
title: The thread behind the ceiling
context: In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, Gārgī questions Yājñavalkya about what underlies the world.
opening: The silk ceiling sags each time somebody says it rests on something else. I have one question left before the floor fills with silk. Where shall we put our fingers?

folds.action: Follow one thread to its peg
folds.arrival: A child pulled the peg free. Now we know what held that corner. The rest of the ceiling still hangs.

folds.action: Leave the last thread loose
folds.arrival: The loose end is long enough for the smallest visitor to reach. She asks what holds the peg.

question: Which part of the ceiling could you still explain if the peg fell out?

name: Epictetus
title: The kettle at the gate
context: Epictetus taught Stoic philosophy. Arrian recorded accounts of his teaching.
opening: My kettle boils just as the gate shuts. The guard cannot move the bell. I can still decide whose cup to warm.

folds.action: Share the water through the bars
folds.arrival: Two cold hands meet round one cup. The gate stays locked. In the morning the guard asks for a second cup.

folds.action: Carry the kettle to the queue
folds.arrival: The back of the line gets tea. By the time the guard comes out there is none left for him.

question: Where did your kettle give someone a choice they could actually use?

name: Zera Yacob
title: The margin that talks back
context: The Hatata, a work of philosophical inquiry in Geʽez, is traditionally attributed to Zera Yacob. Its authorship has been debated.
opening: Someone filed a question under my name. The scribe swears the ink is mine. Good ink. Very poor reason to agree with it.

folds.action: Cover the signature and read it again
folds.arrival: Without a famous name to lean on, the argument kept one listener and lost two. The quiet one asked for the page.

folds.action: Bind the objection beside the page
folds.arrival: The binding bulges. A reader can now find the objection even if they came looking for an authority.

question: Would you trust the same margin if somebody else had signed it?

name: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
title: A key in the gutter
context: Sor Juana wrote poetry and a defence of women's intellectual work in New Spain.
opening: The shelf has a lock and the poem fits under the door. My friend on the other side wants the book. She also wants to keep her job.

folds.action: Slip a verse under the door
folds.arrival: Someone has sung it back with the last line changed. I want to hear that line again.

folds.action: Lend her the key until dawn
folds.arrival: She found a second book I had never read. Neither of us heard the morning bell.

question: Who has to stay awake tonight for that key to be useful?

name: B. R. Ambedkar
title: A thumbprint without a seat
context: Ambedkar chaired the drafting committee for India's Constitution and wrote about caste and exclusion.
opening: They have counted every hand in the room. The people waiting outside are asking who wrote the rule about rooms.

folds.action: Move the hearing to the steps
folds.arrival: A weaver can speak between shifts. Rain blurs the clerk’s record of her last sentence.

folds.action: Give the absentees the next signature
folds.arrival: The draft rests overnight. By morning the excluded workers have changed the very first line.

question: Whose thumbprint could appear on the record without its owner ever getting a turn?

name: Judith Butler
title: The usher's coat
context: Judith Butler's work examines how repeated acts help establish social expectations around gender.
opening: Wear the usher’s coat and everyone hands you a ticket. My friend wore it to keep warm. Now people are obeying a rule nobody remembers making.

folds.action: Trade coats in sight of the queue
folds.arrival: The queue follows the coat halfway across the room. One patron stays with the friend who knows her name.

folds.action: Let each door invent its greeting
folds.arrival: Visitors learn two ways to arrive. The usher asks what happens to people who have to use both doors.

question: What did the usher learn when the coat moved to another pair of shoulders?

name: Ibn al-Haytham
title: The window that borrowed a tree
context: Ibn al-Haytham investigated vision and light in the Book of Optics.
opening: A tree has appeared upside down on the shutter. My assistant wants the branch put back outside before the housekeeper notices.

folds.action: Slide a card across the opening
folds.arrival: The tree disappears one strip at a time. The housekeeper has started moving the card herself.

folds.action: Move the screen toward the pinhole
folds.arrival: The little tree grows sharp enough to count a fork. Nobody has moved the tree outside.

question: How could someone across the island check that the tree outside was still there?

name: Michael Faraday
title: A twitch with no signature
context: Faraday investigated electromagnetic induction and gave public demonstrations of science.
opening: Watch the needle while I move the magnet. The apprentice watching my face sees a fine performance and misses the twitch.

folds.action: Turn the dial toward the apprentice
folds.arrival: She catches a second twitch while I look away. For once the observation belongs to her.

folds.action: Leave a pencil on the moving paper
folds.arrival: The scratch waits for the late shift. They can see when it moved but still need someone who saw what I did.

question: Which movement would the pencil keep if the apprentice blinked?

name: George Washington Carver
title: The second row of beans
context: At Tuskegee, Carver taught agricultural methods including crop rotation.
opening: At the fair they want my tallest plant. A farmer asks what the soil will be like after the fair is gone.

folds.action: Take both beds on the fair map
folds.arrival: The modest plants get a place beside the show row. A farmer recognizes ground much like his own.

folds.action: Mark where next year's crop will go
folds.arrival: The empty row draws laughter until a grower asks to borrow the plan for another season.

question: What would you plant next to the beans to check what helped them?

name: Chien-Shiung Wu
title: The looking-glass mitten
context: Wu led the experimental work that demonstrated parity violation in beta decay.
opening: Two gloves fit a mirror beautifully. My assistant has copied the picture onto the instrument and called the pair a test. Which trace shall travel?

folds.action: Send the two raw traces facing the same way
folds.arrival: The difference survives the turn. A reader can find exactly which mark spoiled the apparent symmetry.

folds.action: Pack the mirror beside the traces
folds.arrival: A visitor turns the glass and catches herself making the same assumption my assistant made.

question: What must both observers agree to face before their traces can be compared?

name: Tu Youyou
title: A word worn thin
context: Tu Youyou drew on historical Chinese medical texts in research that led to artemisinin.
opening: Three copies of a remedy disagree on a verb. A clerk has already rubbed one away to make the shelf tidy. I can still see the dent.

folds.action: Lift the dent into the margin
folds.arrival: The old reading can be compared again. Nobody has to trust the clerk’s memory of the erased word.

folds.action: Put the three copies out of order
folds.arrival: A reader follows the wording instead of the newest cover. She finds two pages descend from the same copy.

question: Which copy changed the way you read the worn word?

name: Robin Wall Kimmerer
title: The bare patch beside the moss
context: Kimmerer is a botanist and member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation whose writing brings plant ecology into conversation with reciprocity.
opening: I came looking for green and passed a brown patch without a glance. Then my boot crushed the moss beside it. Moving my boot and changing what I expect to see are two different repairs.

folds.action: Move the viewing cord back
folds.arrival: A wider circle of moss survives the week. The smallest leaf needs a borrowed lens.

folds.action: Invite the caretaker to set the path
folds.arrival: The path bends around wet ground I had overlooked. The caretaker keeps the authority to close it.

question: Who gets to say when the moss has had enough visitors?

name: Ben Barres
title: The faint cells
context: Barres studied the roles of glia in the nervous system.
opening: Everyone crowded round the bright drawing at my talk. The faint shapes barely made it into the programme. They take up most of my working day.

folds.action: Trace the faint layer on its own sheet
folds.arrival: The support cells fill a whole page. Their positions make sense when a reader lowers it onto the bright drawing.

folds.action: Give the second lamp to the assistant
folds.arrival: A second pair of eyes finds a gap I had filled in from habit. We leave the gap visible.

question: What did the second lamp let the assistant see for themself?

name: Brahmagupta
title: An empty purse with a balance
context: Brahmagupta wrote rules for arithmetic with zero, debts and fortunes.
opening: Our two traders have no coins between them. One still owes the other three. The clerk has painted identical purses on their doors.

folds.action: Hang a debt bead below the beam
folds.arrival: The empty pans look alike until the bead swings below one. Its owner can tell who still owes whom.

folds.action: Walk the ledger backward to the loan
folds.arrival: The clerk sees both purses empty and the loan still alive. He keeps the earlier line with the new one.

question: Who would count the purse as empty even with a debt hanging below it?

name: Al-Khwārizmī
title: A length missing from the cloth
context: Al-Khwarizmi wrote an influential treatise on solving equations.
opening: Half the awning is folded inside a seam. The tailor will cut today if I can give her a rule that travels farther than this stall.

folds.action: Unfold the seam on the bench
folds.arrival: The tailor sees the hidden length. She takes a pattern home that fits this particular awning.

folds.action: Balance strips on both sides of a peg
folds.arrival: The apprentice applies the same move to a different bolt. He still needs the tailor to say where the seam begins.

question: Which length of cloth did the seam hide from your first measurement?

name: Emmy Noether
title: The wheel with no privileged spoke
context: Noether established a connection between continuous symmetries and conservation laws in physics.
opening: The miller painted one spoke gold to show us where the law lives. We turned the wheel. The gold is now at the bottom and the mill still works.

folds.action: Scrape a chalk ring round the turning hub
folds.arrival: Every spoke crosses the same ring. The miller’s daughter wants to know what survives a different kind of turn.

folds.action: Lay tracing paper over two turns
folds.arrival: The spokes exchange places under the tracing. The axle stays put and the gold mark finally earns a rest.

question: What still lined up when the wheel came round again?

name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
title: Numbers in a coat pocket
context: Ramanujan's notebooks preserve extensive results in number theory, often without the derivations.
opening: My coat has a page of patterns and a hole in the pocket. The person who picks it up may have the result and none of the steps.

folds.action: Stitch in a small worked case
folds.arrival: The finder can check the first few terms before deciding whether to chase the rest.

folds.action: Send the surprising line with a blank margin
folds.arrival: Someone fills the margin with a route I never took. Another line stays stubbornly empty.

question: How far would you trust the surprising line on the strength of one worked case?

name: Maryam Mirzakhani
title: A loop that refuses to untie
context: Mirzakhani studied the geometry and dynamics of curved surfaces.
opening: I drew a walk on this curved sheet. The ferryman flattened it for his pocket and now my walker seems to step through a wall.

folds.action: Run a cord along the curved walk
folds.arrival: The ferryman feels where the walk returns. His flat map still squeezes the last bend.

folds.action: Cut a window in a second sheet
folds.arrival: The two drawings meet at the window. Each shows a stretch the other makes hard to see.

question: Where did flattening the walk change the loop you were trying to follow?

name: Autumn Kent
title: A knot with two shadows
context: Kent researches knots, surfaces and three-dimensional geometry.
opening: On the wall this loop crosses itself six times. Turn the lantern and it crosses four. My young rigger has put two prices on the very same rope.

folds.action: Rotate the lamp with the ends tied
folds.arrival: The rigger keeps four shadows and one knot. Her new price tag has room for a drawing angle.

folds.action: Pass a bead along the whole loop
folds.arrival: The bead goes home without jumping a strand. The easiest crossing to draw was the hardest one to follow.

question: Which feature of the knot survived turning the lamp?

name: Sima Qian
title: The runaway's missing page
context: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian tells history through several forms, including individual biographies.
opening: The clerk left enough room for a ruler’s life and half a line for the runner who carried the news. The runner remembers the rain best.

folds.action: Bind the runner's account at the front
folds.arrival: Readers enter the city wet and late. Some ask which ruler was waiting at the gate.

folds.action: Thread the two lives by the same afternoon
folds.arrival: One date leads to two different rooms. The runner’s rain explains a delay that looks deliberate in the palace.

question: If only one page escaped, whose afternoon would survive with it?

name: Anna Komnene
title: The family's chair
context: Anna Komnene wrote the Alexiad, a history centred on the reign of her father Alexios I.
opening: My father’s chair makes the best place to see the gate. It also makes me his daughter telling the story. A visitor has noticed both things.

folds.action: Set another chair by the servants' door
folds.arrival: The second witness saw who waited outside. The gate was hidden from that angle.

folds.action: Mark the first sightline on the plan
folds.arrival: A stranger can judge just how much I could see. It feels rather exposed to leave my chair there.

question: Which part of the room could the family chair never show its occupant?

name: Cheikh Anta Diop
title: The drawer filed under nowhere
context: Diop drew on multiple disciplines to investigate African history.
opening: The colonial index begins this river kingdom's history with a traveller’s visit. Local dates were filed as notes about his voyage. The drawer sticks where somebody forced them in.

folds.action: Refit the drawer round the local dates
folds.arrival: Neighbours open it at their own beginning. An overseas reader asks for a slip between the two calendars.

folds.action: Hang the excavated layer beside the written date
folds.arrival: The mismatch is small enough to overlook on paper. On the wall it starts an argument worth staying for.

question: Which date became visible when the drawer was filed differently?

name: Silvia Rivera Cusicanqui
title: Two colours still wet
context: Rivera Cusicanqui worked with oral history in Bolivia and developed the idea of ch'ixi as a way of thinking about difference that persists.
opening: The printer promises me one perfect colour if I let him stir long enough. The two narrators want to see where their threads touch.

folds.action: Twist the colours into one cord
folds.arrival: From across the hall it looks grey. Up close you can still follow each strand to its own end.

folds.action: Stretch the strands across opposite seats
folds.arrival: A listener moves between the seats. She hears an overlap neither speaker had noticed.

question: What could a listener hear from opposite seats that a single twisted cord might hide?

name: Susan Stryker
title: The box under the chosen name
context: Stryker has worked as a historian and archivist of transgender lives.
opening: A singer requests a box by her stage name. The old index knows a different name. She would like strangers to find her work without finding everything else.

folds.action: Give her the pencil for the public index
folds.arrival: Her chosen entry leads to the songs. She keeps the other slip folded inside her coat.

folds.action: Bind a private cross-reference
folds.arrival: A trusted keeper can reunite the records. A stranger has to ask, and may never learn why.

question: Who needs to find the older record, and who gets to decide how?

name: Te Rangi Hīroa
title: A paddle drawn from above
context: Te Rangi Hīroa, of Ngāti Mutunga descent, studied material culture and served as director of the Bishop Museum.
opening: The cabinet shows every carved line. A canoe builder turns the drawing sideways and asks where a thumb goes. I have a spare sheet.

folds.action: Trace a grip with the builder's leave
folds.arrival: A smudge of charcoal tells the next visitor where pressure falls. The handle in the case stays untouched.

folds.action: Set the drawing at paddling height
folds.arrival: The builder stands in front of it and changes the angle. A sitting visitor asks for a lower stand too.

question: What did placing the paddle at shoulder height reveal about the drawing?

name: Julio C. Tello
title: The pots the catalogue separated
context: Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello investigated Chavín and Paracas, among other sites and cultures.
opening: The cabinet clerk likes straight rows of colour. I need the space between two vessels on the old ground plan. We cannot lift the floor again.

folds.action: Join their cases with the excavation plan
folds.arrival: A reader finds the gap where the vessels once stood. Two similar rims turn out to come from different places.

folds.action: Leave one space empty in the row
folds.arrival: Visitors ask what belongs there. The keeper unfolds the plan before answering.

question: What would it cost to fill the gap with the nearest-looking pot?

name: Zora Neale Hurston
title: The story with a laughing pause
context: Hurston collected folklore and paid close attention to the settings in which stories were told.
opening: I can take the words down beautifully. My pencil cannot tell you who laughed before the last line or why the teller waited for it.

folds.action: Keep the pause in the performance
folds.arrival: The new audience laughs in a different place. The teller gets to set the pace again.

folds.action: Ask the teller to place the laugh in the margin
folds.arrival: The teller draws an arrow to a person, not a word. The reader needs to know who was in the room.

question: Did the pause belong to the teller, the audience, or their moment together?

name: Kathleen Kenyon
title: A line of earth no wider than a finger
context: Kenyon used stratigraphic excavation at Jericho.
opening: The tray is full of lovely finds. My best clue is a dark line in the wall that the next scoop will take away.

folds.action: Draw the wall before filling the tray
folds.arrival: The drawing keeps the order of the layers. The waiting crew loses the last patch of daylight.

folds.action: Leave a narrow strip standing
folds.arrival: A second visitor can feel where the soil changes. The strip hides a little of what lies behind it.

question: Which question about the trench could a later visitor still investigate?

name: Mary Leakey
title: Footsteps after rain
context: Leakey directed investigations of the preserved hominin tracks at Laetoli in Tanzania.
opening: Three tracks cross the soft patch. The painter has already given their makers faces. The length of a step is all I promised.

folds.action: Cast the interval between two prints
folds.arrival: The empty space goes into the case too. A walker tries a shorter stride and gets a different story.

folds.action: Project outlines with the figures left out
folds.arrival: Visitors walk the spacing themselves. One child asks how fast the mud was drying.

question: What could two prints tell you even if you left the walkers out of the picture?

name: Kwang-chih Chang
title: The house beyond the fine bowl
context: Chang studied early Chinese societies through archaeology, including settlements and their relationships.
opening: The collector’s light falls exactly on the painted bowl. My map reaches the small houses where nobody owned one. The light has a hinge.

folds.action: Swing the lamp over the house plan
folds.arrival: The bowl becomes one household among many. Its painting is suddenly much harder to see.

folds.action: Draw a walking route from bowl to doorway
folds.arrival: A visitor follows the clay back to a house. Another asks whose doorway never got a marker.

question: Whose movements around the bowl would the display case conceal?

name: Pāṇini
title: The rule that ate its neighbour
context: Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī describes Sanskrit using a system of interacting grammatical rules.
opening: A single sound changes at the join between two words. The printer applied my rules in reverse order and the result still looks terribly official.

folds.action: Slide one rule strip over the other
folds.arrival: The apprentice sees which instruction gets to the join first. She saves both strips for the next form.

folds.action: Keep the unjoined words on a flap
folds.arrival: A reader lifts the flap and finds the original sounds. The printed line alone had hidden them.

question: Which join changed when the rule strips exchanged places?

name: Ibn Khaldūn
title: The loaf for an impossible army
context: Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah considers how the conditions of social life affect the plausibility of historical reports.
opening: A chronicler has filled a valley with more people than the storekeeper can feed. He says the number came from an excellent book.

folds.action: Build a stack for a day's bread
folds.arrival: The stack fills the storeroom before it feeds the claimed crowd. The baker asks where the missing road would go.

folds.action: Trace the count back through its copies
folds.arrival: Five witnesses shrink to a single borrowed numeral. That still leaves the size of the crowd open.

question: What would another loaf establish that a second copy of the headcount could not?

name: W. E. B. Du Bois
title: The chart that never meets its street
context: Du Bois combined social inquiry, maps and data graphics to study and communicate racial inequality.
opening: The bars fit beautifully. Outside, a woman points to the boundary that cuts her yard in two. Both halves have become different colours.

folds.action: Walk the chart's boundary
folds.arrival: The yard is one place underfoot. The seam in the graphic now has an address.

folds.action: Put her account beside the bar
folds.arrival: The reader can hear what a tidy average costs one household. The overall pattern is still there to inspect.

question: Where on her street did the chart stop describing her day?

name: Mamie Phipps Clark
title: Two toys and a watchful room
context: Mamie Phipps Clark studied children's racial identification and the effects of segregation.
opening: The adults want me to name what a child feels from the toy they reached for. The child was watching us the whole time. My own notebook is part of the room.

folds.action: Record where the adults stood
folds.arrival: The reach stays in the record, along with the audience that could have changed it.

folds.action: Give the child a private second turn
folds.arrival: The second choice differs. Nobody puts either choice beside the child's name.

question: How might the adults’ places have changed what the child felt able to do?

name: Elinor Ostrom
title: A key that belongs to the ditch
context: Ostrom studied how communities make and sustain rules for shared resources.
opening: Our neighbours know which gate sticks. The survey gives the key to a distant clerk because his desk is always occupied.

folds.action: Hang the key by the user roster
folds.arrival: The last water user can open the gate. Two neighbours volunteer to settle a dispute about the roster.

folds.action: Give each shift a seal for repairs
folds.arrival: The clerk can see who noticed a leak. A visitor working between shifts needs somebody to vouch for her.

question: Who could repair the ditch if its key holder missed a shift?

name: Raewyn Connell
title: The chair called ordinary
context: Connell's work examines how institutions produce gender hierarchies and which voices shape social theory.
opening: The manual says a good foreman sounds like this. That voice has got awfully comfortable in the only chair at the table.

folds.action: Turn the chair toward the night crew
folds.arrival: The manual's example has to answer questions from people who never wrote it.

folds.action: Leave the chair empty for one shift
folds.arrival: A quiet worker organises the next cart without taking the seat. The recorder has trouble naming what she did.

question: Whose working day disappears when the chair faces the usual way?

name: Leonardo da Vinci
title: The hinge that draws a wing
context: Leonardo used drawing to investigate movement, anatomy and mechanisms.
opening: My paper bird opens beautifully on the table. At the window a real bird folds its wing a different way. I rather like my hinge. That is the trouble.

folds.action: Trace the living wing's second fold
folds.arrival: The old hinge no longer fits the tracing. The apprentice keeps both in the notebook.

folds.action: Build a paper joint that can slip
folds.arrival: The paper bends where I did not plan. A working hinge has taught us something a pretty sketch concealed.

question: Where did the paper hinge have to give for the wing to move?

name: Katsushika Ōi
title: The lantern behind the sleeve
context: Ōi was an Edo-period Japanese artist known in particular for her treatment of light.
opening: The apprentice painted the face first. Now the lantern is lit and the shadow of a sleeve has become the centre of the room.

folds.action: Move the lantern behind the screen
folds.arrival: The face disappears into shade. Its owner can finally watch without being watched.

folds.action: Paint the edge where the light stops
folds.arrival: The sleeve stays still. A visitor can tell how high the lantern hangs from the edge alone.

question: Which edge belonged to the sleeve and which to the lantern?

name: Claude Cahun
title: Who pressed the shutter
context: Cahun worked with Marcel Moore on images that explored identity and performance.
opening: Two people made this portrait. One stood in the clothes. One waited behind the shutter. The catalogue has room for a single name.

folds.action: Turn the mirror toward the camera stand
folds.arrival: The reflection includes the work behind the image. The sitter loses the perfectly blank background.

folds.action: Write the credit on a reversible mount
folds.arrival: Flip the portrait and a collaborator comes into view. Some visitors never think to turn it.

question: Who else had a hand in the picture outside the frame?

name: Frida Kahlo
title: The mirror nailed above the bed
context: Kahlo made self-portraits drawing on her life and physical experiences in Mexico.
opening: The portrait stand expects a sitter to come to it. My bed has other plans. A mirror and a strong pair of arms might let the painting start here.

folds.action: Tilt the mirror over the pillow
folds.arrival: The face looks straight out from a body at rest. A viewer asks where the artist stood.

folds.action: Bring the canvas within reach of the bed
folds.arrival: A crooked first stroke stays where my hand could reach. The gallery has to lower its usual hook.

question: How did moving the canvas change what the painter could decide?

name: Emily Kame Kngwarreye
title: An invitation with an edge
context: Anmatyerr artist Emily Kam Kngwarray made paintings closely connected to Alhalker Country.
opening: The visitor wants one sentence to carry away from a canvas. We have a public title to share. Nobody promised him every story the painting holds.

folds.action: Give him the public title to take home
folds.arrival: He returns to look at the surface. The title keeps its connection to the artist and place.

folds.action: Leave the speaking time with the custodian
folds.arrival: A smaller group comes back at the offered hour. The custodian chooses what can travel beyond the room.

question: What can a visitor take home when the custodian keeps the speaking time?

name: El Anatsui
title: Cloth that clinks
context: El Anatsui makes large flexible sculptures assembled from small metal components, including bottle closures.
opening: The shipping crate wants this metal hanging folded exactly as it was last time. The installer has a low doorway and a good pair of hands.

folds.action: Let the installer set a new fold
folds.arrival: A sweep of bottle caps catches the light in a place the earlier room never had.

folds.action: Keep a crease from the previous hall
folds.arrival: One ridge travels from wall to wall. The new installer finds another fold to carry its weight.

question: Which crease would you miss if the cloth came with a single hanging diagram?

name: Mozi
title: The bridge for someone's cousin
context: Mozi's ethical arguments include impartial concern for people's welfare.
opening: There is timber for one bridge. I know the people on the left bank. Today the stranger on the right bank needs to cross just as badly.

folds.action: Test the same load on each crossing
folds.arrival: The carpenter sees two equal weights and two different lengths of rope. Equal concern still leaves work to do.

folds.action: Lend the boards by crossing time
folds.arrival: Both banks get a turn. A family with the wrong shift has to ask the others to change the timetable.

question: Who loses a crossing while the test load is on the boards?

name: Hypatia of Alexandria
title: The circle that moved in the copy
context: Hypatia taught mathematics and philosophy in Alexandria.
opening: The student copied the proof carefully. Her circle slipped sideways. The conclusion survived. I would like to know what her hand preserved.

folds.action: Turn the proof until the letters move
folds.arrival: The letters lose their familiar seats. The same relations keep the student's conclusion standing.

folds.action: Leave her drawing beside the neat one
folds.arrival: The crooked diagram is the one another pupil can reconstruct. The polished one still makes the pattern easier to see.

question: What in the circle still held when the labels turned away from you?

name: Ibn Rushd
title: Two hands on one commentary
context: Ibn Rushd wrote extensive philosophical commentaries, including commentaries on Aristotle.
opening: The printer put my explanation in the same type as the older argument. I know which sentence I added. A stranger will have to guess.

folds.action: Cut a narrow window for the older line
folds.arrival: Readers can put a finger on the claim before they reach my gloss. My longer objection spills onto the next page.

folds.action: Give each voice its own hinge
folds.arrival: The pages fold together for a quick reading and pull apart when someone wants to know who said what.

question: Who can answer for each line if you close the commentary's hinge?

name: Anton Wilhelm Amo
title: A pinprick in two columns
context: Amo wrote about the relation between mind and body in eighteenth-century European philosophy.
opening: The table has columns for the body and the mind. A visitor felt the pinprick once. I would like two accounts without making her go through it twice.

folds.action: Let the visitor place the first token
folds.arrival: She marks the experience before the observer marks a reaction. The two tokens land a moment apart.

folds.action: Draw the observer's sightline
folds.arrival: The watcher could see a hand move. Only the visitor could say how the movement felt.

question: Which part of the pinprick account could only the visitor supply?

name: Paulo Freire
title: The notice that talks at people
context: Freire developed a dialogical approach to education rooted in learners' circumstances.
opening: My sign has very clear instructions and an absolutely silent audience. A fish seller has a name for this corner that appears on none of my maps.

folds.action: Let the seller name the first stop
folds.arrival: The new route begins where the market actually meets. The official gate moves to the second line.

folds.action: Trade places at the noticeboard
folds.arrival: I try to follow my own notice carrying her basket. She takes the chalk out of my hand at the difficult turn.

question: Who could change tomorrow's route after the seller took your place?

name: Kwasi Wiredu
title: The word left at the crossing
context: Wiredu examined philosophical concepts across languages, including Akan and English.
opening: Three speakers nodded at the translation. Later I learned they meant two rather different things by agreeing. Our meeting has one bell left.

folds.action: Ask for the word in an everyday exchange
folds.arrival: One speaker uses it to end a quarrel. Another uses it to invite a reply. The translator saves both exchanges.

folds.action: Leave a hinge in the translated line
folds.arrival: The hinge opens onto the original expression. The next interpreter has a place to put a new reading.

question: When did the everyday exchange call for a different word at the crossing?

name: Paul B. Preciado
title: The pass with two boxes
context: Preciado examines how institutions and technologies organise experiences of bodies and gender.
opening: The gatekeeper can describe every traveller except the one at the desk. Our printed pass offers two boxes. The traveller needs a key, not a public inquiry.

folds.action: Issue a key against the task alone
folds.arrival: The visitor gets to the workshop. The old ledger can no longer claim it knows everyone who passed.

folds.action: Let the visitor write the pass label
folds.arrival: The visitor chooses a word and keeps a copy. Others waiting in line can hear the conversation.

question: What does the visitor need the pass to do that its boxes fail to record?

name: Shen Kuo
title: The shell above the sea
context: Shen Kuo discussed what fossils and landforms could suggest about earlier environments.
opening: There is a shell in a mountain wall. The innkeeper would like a tide chart for tonight. I am wondering about a much older shore.

folds.action: Draw the layers around the shell
folds.arrival: The shell acquires neighbours that a single display case erased. The innkeeper keeps tonight's tide chart separate.

folds.action: Walk the ridge for a second exposure
folds.arrival: The next wall bears another trace. The walk has cost a morning and earned a second place to check.

question: What would a second ridge have to show to change your reading of the shell?

name: Carlos Juan Finlay
title: The map with no dates
context: Carlos Finlay proposed a role for mosquitoes in the transmission of yellow fever.
opening: The town remembers a season of fever. Its map puts all the sick houses on one neat afternoon. Families recall quite different weeks.

folds.action: Add a turning wheel for dates
folds.arrival: The reader can see a sequence the flat map buried. Several houses have only an approximate week.

folds.action: Invite families to mark gaps privately
folds.arrival: The map loses a few exact-looking dates. The story of how the town noticed trouble becomes more credible.

question: Whose absence would still go unmarked on the date wheel?

name: Santiago Ramón y Cajal
title: The line between two nerve cells
context: Ramón y Cajal used microscopy and drawing to investigate the structure of the nervous system.
opening: I can draw a line so fine it looks unbroken. The lens gives me two edges and a space too small to settle by eye.

folds.action: Lift the connecting line onto tracing paper
folds.arrival: The reader can remove the proposed connection. The edges I actually saw stay in the drawing.

folds.action: Sketch two separate fields of view
folds.arrival: A repeated shape shows up in both fields. A tempting join in the first drawing vanishes in the second.

question: Which stretch of the connecting line came from your pencil?

name: Janaki Ammal
title: The plant with three names
context: Janaki Ammal investigated plant chromosomes and cultivated plants, including sugarcane.
opening: The gardener, the seller and the cabinet all know this plant. Each label gets it through a different door. Only one tag will fit on the cutting.

folds.action: Tie the grower's name to the cutting
folds.arrival: The person who tended the plant can recognise it. The cabinet keeper asks for a cross-reference.

folds.action: Fit a folding tag to the pot
folds.arrival: The collector opens it and finds three names with their users. The small print sends her looking for a lens.

question: Which name would help the grower find this same plant again?

name: Rachel Carson
title: The quiet morning
context: Carson wrote about the ecological effects of pesticides and the relationships between living things.
opening: A visitor has described the meadow as perfectly empty. I heard him arrive at noon. The dawn listener is still sitting in the grass.

folds.action: Send a dawn and noon listening strip
folds.arrival: Two quiet moments have different sounds. The visitor asks for the date beside each one.

folds.action: Keep a silent space on the sound roll
folds.arrival: People stop waiting for narration long enough to hear a distant bird. One morning cannot settle a season.

question: What else might leave the dawn strip quiet?

name: Fe del Mundo
title: The little chair in the clinic
context: Fe del Mundo worked on children's health and founded a children's hospital in the Philippines.
opening: The register says the child never returned. The parent remembers three visits to a room with no register. There is only one little chair in the new waiting room.

folds.action: Take the register to the outer bench
folds.arrival: A family waiting outside gets counted. The nurse has farther to walk with it.

folds.action: Invite a parent to draw the journey
folds.arrival: The map has six stops where the register had one appointment. The chair goes beside the longest wait.

question: Where on the way to the clinic would a missing visit become invisible?

name: Abdus Salam
title: Two lanterns behind one screen
context: Salam contributed to the theoretical unification of electromagnetic and weak interactions.
opening: The workshop shows two different patterns of light. I suspect they belong to the same frame, but the spare shutters have not arrived.

folds.action: Build a frame that holds both diagrams
folds.arrival: A visitor finds the common marks. The frame also shows precisely where the two diagrams still differ.

folds.action: Reserve a slot for the missing test
folds.arrival: The empty slot makes the prediction visible to a critic before any new result can fill it.

question: What could a new test settle that fitting the diagrams together could not?

name: Lynn Conway
title: The pattern another shop can build
context: Conway helped change how integrated circuits could be designed and taught.
opening: The plan fits the chip. The craftsperson fits the pieces. When the plan is passed on, whose work has a name and whose has become invisible?

folds.action: Label the boundary between the two workshops
folds.arrival: A second builder can locate a mismatch without blaming the person who drew the whole design.

folds.action: Send a small reusable design tile
folds.arrival: The next workshop fits the tile into another job. It has to ask which assumptions travelled with it.

question: Which workshop would first notice a missing instruction on the design tile?

name: Madhava of Sangamagrama
title: The circle that takes all night
context: Madhava is associated with the Kerala mathematical tradition and infinite series used in geometric calculation.
opening: My cord comes closer to the rim with each new piece. The navigator needs a circle before the lantern goes out.

folds.action: Mark the gap after three pieces
folds.arrival: The navigator can judge whether this approximation suits tonight's trip. The missing length stays visible.

folds.action: Give the next watcher the unfinished rule
folds.arrival: The next shift can improve the rim. Tonight's navigator must make do with the shorter cord.

question: What does the gap after three pieces let the next watcher estimate?

name: Ada Lovelace
title: A tune in the pattern cards
context: Lovelace's notes on the Analytical Engine considered operations on symbols beyond ordinary arithmetic.
opening: The loom can carry a pattern for flowers. I wonder what the marks could stand for if the next person wants notes instead.

folds.action: Thread the same pattern through a music roll
folds.arrival: The mechanism repeats the arrangement as sound. It needs a musician to assign the pitches.

folds.action: Leave the meaning key beside the loom
folds.arrival: A weaver reads flowers and a musician reads intervals. Both can point to the same repeat.

question: What does the loom need from a musician before its pattern becomes a tune?

name: Sofia Kovalevskaya
title: The top under the table
context: Kovalevskaya made mathematical contributions to the study of rotating bodies.
opening: The spinning top rolls under the table just when our curve gets interesting. The child who found it knows how it wobbled but has no graph.

folds.action: Trace the wobble beside the drawn curve
folds.arrival: The trace meets the prediction for part of a turn. A scratch on the top explains where they part.

folds.action: Give the child the release cord
folds.arrival: A new starting angle changes the whole dance. The curve is useful again once its starting condition is marked.

question: Who saw a difference between the release and the drawn curve?

name: Alan Turing
title: The reply through the curtain
context: Turing proposed the imitation game in discussing machine intelligence.
opening: Two replies have come from behind the curtain. One is witty. One is slow. The audience thinks it can tell who is there before asking either anything interesting.

folds.action: Swap the order in which replies are read
folds.arrival: The favourite changes seats without changing a word. The audience starts to listen for better evidence.

folds.action: Let both questioners ask a follow-up
folds.arrival: The follow-ups uncover a misunderstanding. They still leave open what it would mean to understand.

question: What changed when a questioner could ask a second question?

name: Katherine Johnson
title: The number that brings them home
context: Johnson calculated and checked trajectories for US space missions.
opening: Three desks give me the same landing point. They all used the same sheet of figures. The pilot wants to know whether that makes three checks.

folds.action: Rebuild one step on a clean sheet
folds.arrival: One independent line now meets the machine's curve. We know exactly how much was checked.

folds.action: Draw a band around the landing point
folds.arrival: The crew sees the range it should prepare for. Nobody mistakes a pencil dot for a promise.

question: Which uncertainty would matter most to the crew waiting at the landing point?

name: June Huh
title: The orchard of linked paths
context: June Huh works on connections between combinatorics and algebraic geometry.
opening: The gardener draws trees. I draw connections. We are trying to tell whether two patterns that look different admit the same arrangements.

folds.action: Twist the paths without untying them
folds.arrival: The orchard changes shape while every neighbour stays connected. The labels survive the move.

folds.action: Count arrangements on the smallest corner
folds.arrival: The gardener catches a repeating count. Whether it extends to the whole orchard remains a live question.

question: What would have to stay connected before you could use the small corner to reason about the orchard?

name: Ban Zhao
title: The chapter at the edge of the roll
context: Ban Zhao contributed to completing the Book of Han.
opening: The last compiler left a list unfinished. An easy hand could make my additions look like his. I know his system well enough to do it.

folds.action: Change the heading where the hands change
folds.arrival: The new section keeps the old arrangement. A reader can tell where my judgement entered it.

folds.action: Leave the unfinished line visible
folds.arrival: The break tells a family history of the work. A hurried reader must turn farther to find the completed entry.

question: Who deserves a credit at the join between the two hands?

name: Al-Biruni
title: A mountain and two sightlines
context: Al-Biruni investigated astronomical and geographical measurement, including the dimensions of the Earth.
opening: The mountain does not move when we change our instruments. Our readings do. The travelling party has room for a sketch or another instrument case.

folds.action: Fold the two sightlines into a single sketch
folds.arrival: A distant reader can reconstruct the angle. A crease has to stand in for the mountain.

folds.action: Put a second observer at the lower station
folds.arrival: The observers disagree by a small amount. That difference gives the next party a tolerable range.

question: What could comparing two stations settle about the mountain?

name: C. L. R. James
title: The scorebook missed the crowd
context: James's Beyond a Boundary examines cricket through society, history and personal experience.
opening: Every run made the scorebook. The boundary rope divided the spectators too. You will miss half this match if you take only the score away.

folds.action: Seat the storyteller at the rope
folds.arrival: The match sounds different from either side. The score still tells when the cheer rose.

folds.action: Pin a crowd ticket to the scorecard
folds.arrival: The price of a seat travels with the final number. A reader asks who watched from the street.

question: Which part of the match would disappear if only the scorecard survived?

name: Wang Gungwu
title: A home address across water
context: Wang Gungwu has written extensively on migration and the histories of Chinese communities overseas.
opening: The clerk is stamping a family's registration paper. One home port, he says. They make a living between three. One port would make his index quick and one part of their life disappear.

folds.action: Thread the three ports in travelling order
folds.arrival: A child follows the route to a grandparent the single label had lost.

folds.action: File the family at the port they name
folds.arrival: Their chosen home stays legible. A second family making the same voyage chooses differently.

question: Whose idea of home did the port filing system preserve?

name: Michel-Rolph Trouillot
title: The silence before the shelf
context: Trouillot examined how power shapes the production of histories and silences.
opening: The keeper wants to know which record was lost. I want to know who never had a record made about them in the first place.

folds.action: Follow the empty space back to the intake desk
folds.arrival: The first silence occurred before the box existed. A better shelf alone could never repair it.

folds.action: Keep the unanswered request with the box
folds.arrival: Visitors can hear what the archive cannot supply. The family decides whether to leave a name.

question: At which desk did the silence first enter the box?

name: Ennigaldi-Nanna
title: The curator's second label
context: Ennigaldi-Nanna is associated with a collection of antiquities and collection labels at Ur.
opening: An old brick has turned up with an old description. A trainee has dated the brick from the label. I have two clay stands and one small lamp.

folds.action: Put the label on its own stand
folds.arrival: The brick and its explanation acquire separate histories. A visitor asks who assembled them.

folds.action: Shine the lamp across both surfaces
folds.arrival: The different marks become easy to see. The trainee makes two rubbings instead of one.

question: Which part of what you learned came from the curator's label itself?

name: We'wha
title: The cloth in the wrong drawer
context: We'wha was a Zuni lhamana and a skilled weaver and potter.
opening: Visitors see the finished weave. One visitor reaches for a meaning nobody has offered to share. The loom is mine to demonstrate; the drawer can stay shut.

folds.action: Let the maker choose a public technique
folds.arrival: People see how tension changes the cloth. The closed drawer keeps the boundary the maker set.

folds.action: Bring a second plain practice band
folds.arrival: A learner can handle the practice weave and return the original to its keeper.

question: How could someone learn from the practice band and still respect what the maker kept?

name: Ella Cara Deloria
title: A relation hidden by the translation
context: Ella Cara Deloria studied and documented Dakota language and kinship.
opening: The interpreter has given two relatives the same English label. It will get a parcel there. It will not tell the guest how to address the person who opens it.

folds.action: Let the host introduce the guest
folds.arrival: The parcel arrives after the proper greeting. The guest remembers a relationship that never fit on the tag.

folds.action: Leave the kin term with a spoken example
folds.arrival: The interpreter can hear the word in company. A stranger still needs an introduction.

question: What changed in the welcome when the host introduced the guest?

name: Dorothy Garrod
title: The ledge above the trench
context: Garrod investigated archaeological sequences at Mount Carmel.
opening: The tray looks as if every fragment came from one room. Our notebooks call it three visits to the same patch of ground.

folds.action: Stand the section drawing upright
folds.arrival: A layer becomes a place in a sequence again. The prettiest fragment loses its privileged spot.

folds.action: Return the finds to a scaled floor mat
folds.arrival: The crew sees where two layers overlapped. One uncertain piece sits beside the mat.

question: Which position of the find would disappear in a list of names?

name: Yuri Knorozov
title: The glyph that borrowed a sound
context: Knorozov identified a phonetic component in the writing of the ancient Maya.
opening: A painted sign looks like a creature. In this neighbouring line its sound may be doing the work. My printer wants one creature for the glossary.

folds.action: Print the two settings side by side
folds.arrival: A reader tries a sound across both lines. The creature alone never supplied that test.

folds.action: Leave a sliding cover over the image
folds.arrival: With the picture covered, the surrounding signs still give a clue. One reading remains uncertain.

question: Which setting would you want to see before assigning the glyph a sound?

name: Epeli Hauʻofa
title: The blue space between homes
context: Hauʻofa's writing invited readers to see Oceanian islands as connected through the sea.
opening: The clerk has shaded the sea as empty space between little dots of land. My friends have filled that space with journeys and family visits.

folds.action: Run the route cord across the blue
folds.arrival: The farthest dots become neighbours along a regular voyage. A traveller asks about the wind on the return.

folds.action: Begin the map on a moving deck
folds.arrival: The islands move around the traveller's position. The same sea now has several centres.

question: What became a destination when you began the map on a deck?

name: Shadreck Chirikure
title: The fence around the furnace
context: Chirikure's archaeological work includes African metallurgy, heritage and Great Zimbabwe.
opening: The old furnace is in the register. The people who recognise its working marks are outside the fence. There is a chair on only one side.

folds.action: Take a drawing beyond the fence
folds.arrival: A local craftsperson adds a detail the plan missed and chooses which detail to keep private.

folds.action: Move the meeting to the gate
folds.arrival: The specialists can compare interpretations in person. The visit takes longer than the curator planned.

question: Who could question the drawing when the meeting moved to the gate?

name: Laurent Clerc
title: The speech with the lights off
context: Laurent Clerc was a Deaf teacher who helped establish a school for Deaf students in Hartford.
opening: The director wants darkness for the big speech. In the dark my hands vanish from the front row. The audience still deserves the surprise.

folds.action: Light the signing space from the side
folds.arrival: The hands remain clear while the set disappears. One watcher sees a detail the voice alone never carries.

folds.action: Bring the speaker into the audience circle
folds.arrival: People can face the hands directly. The director has to restage the final entrance.

question: Which seat gives a signer and a listener a clear line of sight to each other?

name: Maria Montessori
title: The shelf my pupil cannot reach
context: Montessori developed educational environments in which children could choose and manipulate materials independently.
opening: A little builder knows exactly which shape she needs. I have put it on a handsome shelf a handspan too high. She keeps being praised for asking me.

folds.action: Lower one shelf to her reach
folds.arrival: She finishes the tower and takes it down without me. I finally see which piece she reaches for next.

folds.action: Give her a tray to arrange herself
folds.arrival: Her order makes sense to her hands. The next builder rearranges it again.

question: What can the pupil now choose without waiting for someone taller?

name: Lev Vygotsky
title: The bridge with a borrowed finger
context: Vygotsky investigated learning through social interaction and the support of more capable partners.
opening: The two ends meet while my finger holds the arch. The child wants to show her brother the trick when I have gone.

folds.action: Slide my support out one block at a time
folds.arrival: She catches the sag herself and changes the base. Her brother sees the arch stand on the second try.

folds.action: Let her coach my clumsy hands
folds.arrival: I build it badly enough to need her words. She finds a way to explain the one move she could not name.

question: At which block could the learner stop borrowing your finger?

name: Frantz Fanon
title: The waiting room with two entrances
context: Fanon was a psychiatrist and writer who examined the lived effects of colonialism.
opening: The register uses the same polite words at both doors. Walk through them and you wait in quite different rooms. Someone has to carry that difference back.

folds.action: Sit in each queue for a turn
folds.arrival: The time slips bear different waits under the same heading. A clerk asks who gets to choose a door.

folds.action: Let visitors mark the route they actually took
folds.arrival: The plan fills with detours absent from the official map. Some visitors fold their slips to keep them private.

question: Which distance on the floor mattered more than the number of seats?

name: Amartya Sen
title: The ticket no one can spend
context: Sen's capability approach draws attention to what people are actually able to do and to be.
opening: We handed out identical ferry tickets. One passenger cannot reach the stairs. The treasurer has recorded a perfectly equal gift.

folds.action: Walk the trip with the folded ticket
folds.arrival: The ticket stays unused at the first step. The treasurer sees what the fare column left out.

folds.action: Give the passenger the route pencil
folds.arrival: The new line reaches a ramp. It is longer and requires the last ferry to wait.

question: What could still keep the passenger from spending a perfectly valid ticket?

name: Deirdre McCloskey
title: The trader's small adjective
context: McCloskey has studied rhetoric and persuasion in economics.
opening: The pitch has a number and a wonderfully persuasive adjective. Our buyer remembers the adjective as though it had been measured.

folds.action: Chalk the number without the sales pitch
folds.arrival: The stall looks plainer. The buyer asks what the number measures before paying.

folds.action: Give the rival trader the same figures
folds.arrival: The rival tells a different story with an identical total. The buyer can now hear the rhetorical choice.

question: What work was the trader's small adjective doing beside the number?

name: Temple Grandin
title: The shadow across the passage
context: Grandin worked on livestock handling facilities with attention to how animals perceive their surroundings.
opening: The yard measures the width of this passage and declares it clear. At ground level a strip of shadow stops the animals short.

folds.action: Walk the route at their eye level
folds.arrival: The dark stripe fills the view. The keeper moves a lamp and watches the next crossing.

folds.action: Record where the herd first hesitates
folds.arrival: Several pauses fall at one place. One animal passes smoothly, complicating a neat explanation.

question: What changed about the passage when you looked from the herd's height?

name: Enheduanna
title: The name on the other face
context: The disk from Ur names Enheduanna. Her historical office and the attribution of particular texts involve different kinds of evidence.
opening: The carved disk has two faces. The guide shows the procession, calls the speaker anonymous and moves on. My name is on the side facing the wall.

folds.action: Turn the stand so the dedication can be seen
folds.arrival: The named priestess becomes visible. The inscription supports an identity, while attribution of a poem still needs its own evidence.

folds.action: Set a reading mirror behind the disk
folds.arrival: The scene and name stay together. The reader has to learn how to follow a reversed line.

question: What did seeing the dedication establish about the disk, and what remains open about the poem?

name: Mimar Sinan
title: The whisper under the dome
context: Sinan designed major Ottoman buildings, including mosques with large domes.
opening: A builder shows me the dome's perfect outline. A child underneath hears her own whisper return from the wrong side of the hall.

folds.action: Walk a whisper round the floor
folds.arrival: Two listeners hear different returns under the same roof. The drawing gains a pair of listening places.

folds.action: Hang a thread from the centre
folds.arrival: The shape finds its centre. The whisper comes back elsewhere and the builder keeps both marks.

question: Which listener could hear the whisper from a place you never stood?

name: Artemisia Gentileschi
title: The hand holding the lamp
context: Gentileschi painted figures taking decisive action and used strong contrasts of light and shade.
opening: My sitter is painted with one hand hidden. A patron has already decided she is helpless. The light can still move before the paint dries.

folds.action: Bring the working hand into light
folds.arrival: A viewer notices the strength in its grip. The face now keeps a secret the brighter version gave away.

folds.action: Keep the hand hidden and shift the gaze
folds.arrival: The sitter looks back at the viewer. Two visitors disagree about who holds the power in the room.

question: Who appears to direct the scene after you move the light?

name: Yayoi Kusama
title: The dot beyond the frame
context: Kusama's work includes repeated dot patterns and installations using mirrors.
opening: The keeper counted every dot on a panel and declared the work finished. I can see the pattern escaping into the polished floor.

folds.action: Place a mirror at the edge
folds.arrival: The count stretches away from the panel. A visitor steps aside to find where the repetition begins.

folds.action: Leave a single unmarked corner
folds.arrival: The little patch changes how the whole field feels. A child starts counting the spaces between dots.

question: What would count as the edge of the pattern from the visitor's position?

name: Ibrahim El-Salahi
title: A line halfway into a letter
context: El-Salahi explored relationships between Arabic calligraphy and modern painting.
opening: The printer asks whether the mark is writing or a drawing. His trays have one compartment for each. My line has already crossed the divider.

folds.action: Print the line across the fold
folds.arrival: A reader turns the sheet sideways and sees the letter again. The fold stays in the picture.

folds.action: Let two readers hang it differently
folds.arrival: One hanging favours rhythm, the other a familiar stroke. A third visitor can walk between them.

question: Where would a second reader put the hinge between a line and a letter?

name: Nam June Paik
title: The television watching itself
context: Paik worked with video, including installations using closed-circuit television.
opening: This screen watches a camera pointed at the screen. My assistant waves from outside the loop and is offended that nobody waves back.

folds.action: Tilt the camera toward the assistant
folds.arrival: The visitor enters the picture. The endless tunnel shortens to make room.

folds.action: Delay the feed by one beat
folds.arrival: A visitor sees a wave after her own hand is still. The camera has made a small past she can watch.

question: Which part of the picture did the delay change for the assistant?

name: Zaha Hadid
title: The ramp in the paper city
context: Hadid developed architectural designs known for unconventional spatial forms.
opening: The building committee chose my sweeping ramp from the plan. A model visitor meets a blank wall at the turn. The people with a vote saw it from above. Who gets to test it from below?

folds.action: Push a bead along the inside turn
folds.arrival: The bead catches at one point the overhead drawing flatters. A builder leaves space there.

folds.action: Cut the wall at the model's eye line
folds.arrival: The view opens for a small traveller. The sweep loses a length of uninterrupted wall.

question: Where would a person on the ramp see something different from the model maker?

name: Kent Monkman
title: The borrowed pose
context: Cree artist Kent Monkman reworks imagery and conventions from European and North American history painting.
opening: The gallery loves the composition. A Cree artist can recognise whose version of history the pose once served. There is room for someone else to look back.

folds.action: Reverse the line of the spectators' gaze
folds.arrival: The figure once shown as scenery now studies the visitors. The old composition is still recognisable.

folds.action: Place the earlier picture within sight
folds.arrival: Visitors see what the new scene is answering. Some have to turn round twice.

question: Who can look back when the spectators change places?

name: Mencius
title: The child at the rail
context: Mencius used the example of a child in danger to explore the beginnings of moral concern.
opening: Someone reached out before any rule was read. Our clerk wants to turn that instant into a law for every crossing. The child is safe and listening.

folds.action: Let the helper describe the instant
folds.arrival: What moved a hand can be heard. It still leaves open what the gate ought to require of strangers.

folds.action: Test the rule on a quiet crossing
folds.arrival: A guard follows the rule and finds nobody in danger. The child asks whether care can wait for a bell.

question: How could you tell whether the quiet crossing called for the same act?

name: Han Feizi
title: The tally that flatters its keeper
context: Han Fei wrote about laws, incentives, officials and political authority.
opening: The gatekeeper who counts departures also wins the prize for an empty queue. His count is impeccable. Two people wait round the corner.

folds.action: Give arrivals their own tally stick
folds.arrival: The two tallies cross at the gate and part round the corner. The keeper can explain the difference.

folds.action: Change what the gatekeeper gets to report
folds.arrival: Waiting time replaces the vanishing line. A visitor who leaves early is still easy to miss.

question: Which arrivals never reach the keeper's tally?

name: Al-Ghazālī
title: The wick after the spark
context: Al-Ghazali examined what repeated observations can establish about causal necessity.
opening: Every time the spark comes the wick catches. The lamp tender says he has seen necessity with his own eyes. I ask him to point to what he actually saw.

folds.action: Keep a strip for each observed sequence
folds.arrival: The order repeats reliably. The tender leaves room for a word about what binds the events.

folds.action: Give a second watcher an unlit wick
folds.arrival: The watcher can describe the expectation before anything happens. The expectation and the flame occupy different moments.

question: What did watching the unlit wick add to the sequence you already had?

name: Ayn Rand
title: The maker's name at the hinge
context: Rand wrote about individual creative achievement, self-interest and political authority.
opening: The council wants to put its crest over a maker's signature on a public gate. The maker wants the work seen and the decision to remain hers.

folds.action: Leave the signature on the working hinge
folds.arrival: Every opening shows who designed it. The neighbours who kept the gate working request space for their names.

folds.action: Let the maker set the terms of display
folds.arrival: The gate stays closed for a meeting. The maker chooses what taking public credit should commit her to.

question: Who must ask permission if the hinge goes on public display?

name: Simone Weil
title: The minute with no answer
context: Weil explored attention as an ethical practice in relation to other people.
opening: A woman has waited all morning to speak. Everyone has prepared a solution for her. She has not yet finished her first sentence.

folds.action: Set down the clerk's response slip
folds.arrival: The silence lasts long enough for her real request. It is smaller and harder than the prepared answer.

folds.action: Give her the next speaking bell
folds.arrival: The others can go back to work. She controls when the room returns to listen.

question: What room did leaving the response slip blank give the speaker?

name: Karl Popper
title: A prediction written in pencil
context: Popper argued for testing scientific claims against observations that could count against them.
opening: The forecaster always rubs out the pencil line after the tide comes in. Every surviving forecast fits beautifully. Tonight we have one dry envelope.

folds.action: Seal a prediction before the bell
folds.arrival: Tomorrow's mismatch survives in the envelope. The forecaster can now revise a method with a reason.

folds.action: Mark a result that would make us stop
folds.arrival: The crew agrees on a warning mark ahead of time. A result just below it becomes their hardest case.

question: Which result would make you reopen the prediction you sealed?

name: Thomas Kuhn
title: The speck every chart scrubbed away
context: Kuhn examined how exemplars, anomalies and changing frameworks shape scientific practice.
opening: Apprentices all clean the same speck from the sky chart. The new watcher has circled it. She knows the old chart well enough to fear being laughed at.

folds.action: Keep a run of the uncleaned charts
folds.arrival: The speck moves in a pattern over the week. The old chart still works for most of the sky.

folds.action: Lend the new watcher one telescope hour
folds.arrival: A different way of sorting the sightings takes shape. Another project loses its hour.

question: What did keeping the uncleaned charts cost the next watcher?

name: Sylvia Wynter
title: The painted outline called everyone
context: Wynter examined how historically specific ideas about humanity come to be treated as universal.
opening: A form asks whether every visitor fits the painted outline. Its maker drew himself. At the desk a whole queue is learning what the word everyone costs.

folds.action: Let a visitor trace the maker's outline
folds.arrival: The supposed universal shape gains a maker and a date. More people can ask how it became the rule.

folds.action: Remove the outline from the doorway
folds.arrival: Visitors pass freely. The old form goes into an archive where someone can still ask whom it excluded.

question: Who had to change shape to fit the painted doorway?

name: Albert Einstein
title: Two clocks along the quay
context: Einstein examined simultaneity and clock synchronisation in special relativity.
opening: The quay master promises that both bells sounded together. The messenger who compared them had to travel between the towers. That journey belongs in the drawing.

folds.action: Mark the path the signals travelled
folds.arrival: The drawing now tells a reader how the clocks were compared. A fast reply and a slow one leave different marks.

folds.action: Put a listener midway between the towers
folds.arrival: The listener can give an account from one place. A moving passenger wants to know which clock governs her ticket.

question: Which clock reading depends on where the listener stood?

name: Niels Bohr
title: Two windows for one lamp
context: Bohr developed the principle of complementarity in quantum physics.
opening: The instruments fit the bench one at a time. A visitor wants both readings printed as though the lamp faced both arrangements at once.

folds.action: Hinge the two bench diagrams together
folds.arrival: The reader can switch arrangements. Each drawing keeps the conditions that gave its reading.

folds.action: Put a label on the empty instrument slot
folds.arrival: The absence explains why the second reading cannot be reported for this run. A second run can still be made.

question: What would you need to learn before you could put the two views in one diagram?

name: Barbara McClintock
title: The kernels that broke the neat row
context: McClintock investigated changing patterns of inheritance in maize.
opening: My maize drawing has a patch of unexpected colour. The cleaner offers to repaint it to match the others. That little patch is the reason I saved the ear.

folds.action: Map every patch before sorting
folds.arrival: The pattern survives the harvest. A second ear gives the reader something to compare.

folds.action: Keep one whole ear with its field note
folds.arrival: The case holds less variety. It keeps a connection the prettier row of loose kernels had lost.

question: Which kernel would go missing if you sorted before you mapped the ear?

name: Lynn Margulis
title: The passenger inside the cell
context: Margulis developed the endosymbiotic account of the origins of structures in eukaryotic cells.
opening: The illustrator drew the cell as a single kingdom. A little structure inside it has a history the kingdom's neat border hides.

folds.action: Draw a second family line inside the border
folds.arrival: Two histories now fit in one cell. The artist needs a different kind of line to say where the evidence runs out.

folds.action: Put the competing diagrams under a flap
folds.arrival: The older picture stays available for comparison. A student can point to the detail that changed the explanation.

question: What observation would help you decide between the two family lines?

name: Richard Dawkins
title: The ledger that counts generations
context: Dawkins popularised a gene-centred view of evolution.
opening: One book follows individual creatures. Another follows a trait across a family. A small change looks like a triumph in one book and vanishes from the other.

folds.action: Follow the trait across three family branches
folds.arrival: The trait persists after one branch ends. The reader must decide what the chosen unit made visible.

folds.action: Carry both books to the same observation
folds.arrival: The field watcher can describe one action at two scales. Neither ledger contains the whole animal.

question: Which claim survives when both books describe the same observation?

name: Joan Roughgarden
title: The fish outside the caption
context: Roughgarden studied the diversity of animal sexual behaviour and debated explanations for it.
opening: The keeper's caption gives the fish two fixed roles. The careful observer at the tank has seen behaviour that crosses the printed line.

folds.action: Make room for the uncaptioned observation
folds.arrival: The keeper can recognise a new pattern on the next visit. The original caption is now something to test.

folds.action: Write a second caption for another group
folds.arrival: The two captions work in different settings. A visitor who tries to generalise has to name the setting first.

question: Whose later observation would make you reopen the caption?

name: Chanda Prescod-Weinstein
title: The faintest visitor on the graph
context: Prescod-Weinstein studies particle physics and cosmology and writes about participation in science.
opening: Our plot leaves room for a possible particle. The person who found the gap in our assumptions had to borrow her hour at the board. I want the empty space and the hour remembered.

folds.action: Keep the empty band on the graph
folds.arrival: A future observation can narrow the band. The legend says plainly that nobody has detected the proposed particle here.

folds.action: Send the calculation with its working credits
folds.arrival: The critic knows whom to ask about a mistaken assumption. The invisible labour gains a name.

question: Who can check the empty band if the working credits travel with it?

name: Seki Takakazu
title: The wooden tablet under the total
context: Seki made important contributions to algebra in the Japanese wasan tradition.
opening: The carpenter can repeat my number. She wants the arrangement that lets her use the method on a different frame.

folds.action: Fit the rows into a sliding tray
folds.arrival: She changes a coefficient and keeps the arrangement. A scratch tells her which row she moved.

folds.action: Leave the worked frame beside the new one
folds.arrival: The carpenter sees the correspondence at a glance. A frame with another joint will need a fresh comparison.

question: What would a later counter learn from the frame that the total hides?

name: Wang Zhenyi
title: An eclipse in the back room
context: Wang Zhenyi studied astronomy and used physical demonstrations to explain eclipses.
opening: Clouds covered the sky on demonstration day. I have a lamp, a ball and a round table. The child nearest the lamp sees something I cannot.

folds.action: Let the child move the ball's shadow
folds.arrival: The little eclipse crosses the table. It explains the alignment while leaving real distances open.

folds.action: Mark two viewing positions on the floor
folds.arrival: One watcher stands in shadow, one in light. The disagreement finally has an address.

question: Whose view would change if the ball stayed still and only the observer moved?

name: David Hilbert
title: The rulebook before the first move
context: Hilbert explored axiom systems, mathematical proof and the foundations of mathematics.
opening: The token game has lovely precise rules. I want to know what follows from them before the potter spends a week carving pieces.

folds.action: Play out a short proof on the tiles
folds.arrival: A spectator can check each move. The line settles one claim about these rules.

folds.action: Pin the starting rules above the board
folds.arrival: The next player changes one rule in plain sight. A conclusion that once held now needs another proof.

question: Which move stops being justified if you lift one starting rule from the board?

name: L. E. J. Brouwer
title: A bridge you can actually build
context: Brouwer developed intuitionism with an emphasis on mathematical construction.
opening: The keeper says that assuming there is no crossing leads to a contradiction. So there must be a crossing. I have a traveller with one plank who needs to know how to build it.

folds.action: Place the first plank and show the next move
folds.arrival: The traveller can reproduce the crossing. Each plank costs another step of work.

folds.action: Mark exactly what the existence claim gives
folds.arrival: The map promises a crossing and shows no footpath yet. The traveller asks the keeper to keep searching.

question: When is being told a bridge exists enough for somebody who needs to cross?

name: Kurt Gödel
title: The seal that certifies every seal
context: Gödel established incompleteness results for certain formal systems strong enough to express arithmetic.
opening: The office has asked its rulebook to vouch for everything the book can do. It is a much bigger request than checking the clerk’s last sum.

folds.action: Set the checked sum apart from the grand promise
folds.arrival: The clerk can defend this result. The margin beside the promise is still open.

folds.action: Move the check to another rulebook
folds.arrival: A second office can ask questions the first cannot settle internally. Now the second book's assumptions are visible too.

question: What reason do you have to trust the second rulebook's seal?

name: Julia Robinson
title: The machine promised every answer
context: Robinson contributed to the work that ultimately answered Hilbert's tenth problem about a general decision procedure.
opening: The machine seller promises a method for every equation on the rack. The little equations it has solved fill his window. I have brought him the word every.

folds.action: Separate the solved cards from the universal claim
folds.arrival: His stack of successes stays impressive. It no longer carries a guarantee about every future card.

folds.action: Hang a question about the promised procedure
folds.arrival: The buyer can inspect what the seller promises will always terminate. One tedious calculation becomes a question about a whole class.

question: Which promise about tomorrow's cards goes beyond today's solved pile?

name: Alexander Grothendieck
title: The map folded around a family of maps
context: Grothendieck developed new structural approaches in algebraic geometry.
opening: The navigator wants me to repair one chart. I have noticed a family resemblance that could repair the next chart too. Her boat leaves today.

folds.action: Repair the one chart at the torn fold
folds.arrival: The boat can leave with a working chart. The resemblance waits as a pencil note for the next maker.

folds.action: Build a frame for comparing the family
folds.arrival: A shared shape emerges across the charts. The boat must borrow a chart while the frame dries.

question: What difference between two maps survives repairing just one fold?

name: Ron Eglash
title: The pattern seen from the hill
context: Eglash has studied recursive mathematical designs and their social contexts.
opening: A visitor sees a repeating layout and says he knows how it was made. The people who laid it out are still here and can choose what to tell him.

folds.action: Ask the makers which part may be modelled
folds.arrival: One public pattern travels with its place and permission. A private detail stays on the hill.

folds.action: Try the proposed rule on a practice layout
folds.arrival: The little model resembles the view. Its success cannot tell us what the original makers intended.
